title: Ethics in epidemics, emergencies and disasters: research, surveillance and patient care: training manual

toc.title: Contributors
Acknowledgements
Introduction
Overview: Ethics in epidemics, emergencies and disasters
Research and surveillance
Core competence 1: Ability to analyse the boundaries between public health practice, including surveillance, and research and their ethical implications in emergencies
Learning objective 1.1: Distinguish between public health surveillance and public health research.
Learning objective 1.2: Identify the scope of activities that could qualify as “research” during emergency response and would normally require research ethics review.
Learning objective 1.3: Demonstrate understanding of the ethical principles and requirements addressed in current normative instruments relative to research and surveillance in emergencies.
Learning objective 1.4: Identify the shortcomings of current normative instruments for use in emergency situations, and evaluate alternatives.
Core competence 2: Ability to define adequate processes for ethics review in public health interventions, surveillance and research in emergencies
Learning objective 2.1: Describe “standard” procedures that should govern an ethics review of research activities, including public health research.
Learning objective 2.2: Identify circumstances in which public health surveillance activities should possibly undergo formal ethics review.
Learning objective 2.3: Describe possible variations to standard procedures of ethics review that are applicable to research in emergencies.
Core competence 3: Ability to identify conflict between the common good and individual autonomy in surveillance during emergency response
Learning objective 3.1: Identify possible harm and benefit to individuals and communities resulting from public health practice and surveillance.
Learning objective 3.2: Assess the factors to be considered in determining when public health surveillance requires explicit informed consent from individuals or communities.
Learning objective 3.3: Evaluate the measures required to protect privacy and confidentiality in an emergency.
Learning objective 3.4: Describe specific measures required to protect and collect data and biological materials during public health surveillance.
Learning objective 3.5: Describe circumstances in which the common good might overrule individual autonomy during public health surveillance.
Core competence 4: Ability to identify conflict between the common good and individual autonomy in research and clinical trials during emergency response
Learning objective 4.1: Identify potential harm and benefit to individuals and communities resulting from conducting research in emergencies.
Learning objective 4.2: Discuss moral theories, and identify frameworks applicable to research in emergencies.

Learning objective 4.3: Explain the current norms under which a waiver of consent could be deemed acceptable for research in critical care settings, and assess when they could be applicable to research in emergencies.
Learning objective 4.4: Explain the processes required to improve informed consent to research in emergencies, with particular consideration of traditional communities and low‑resource settings.
Core competence 5: Ability to explain how publication ethics are related to public health surveillance or research in emergencies
Learning objective 5.1: Explain the conditions in which data gathered during public health surveillance or routine clinical management can be published as scientific knowledge.
Learning objective 5.2: Explain what is meant by “publication bias” and how it might affect the response to emergencies.
Learning objective 5.3: Explain the ethical obligations of researchers, public health practitioners and publishers regarding ownership of scientific data.
Patient care
Core competence 6: Ability to define ethically relevant criteria for triage, resource allocation and standard of care in emergency response
Learning objective 6.1: Discuss ethical frameworks and criteria for triage and rationing in emergencies.
Learning objective 6.2: Understand how criteria for standards of care and treatment can be altered during emergencies.
Learning objective 6.3: Identify issues of benefit‑sharing with communities under public health surveillance.
Learning objective 6.4: Identify issues of equity of access to unproven treatments during research in the course of emergency response.
Core competence 7: Ability to discuss the professional duties of health care workers during public health surveillance or research in emergencies

Learning objective 7.1: Distinguish three ethics frameworks: medical care ethics, public health ethics and research ethics, and explore the ways in which the values and principles that guide these frameworks diverge or overlap.
Learning objective 7.2: Explain what is meant by “therapeutic misconception” and how it could affect the duties of health care workers in emergencies.
Learning objective 7.3: Explain the potential conflicts of interest of health care workers participating in emergency research activities.

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the manual's aim of providing training material on ethics in research, surveillance and patient care during epidemics, emergencies and disasters. It recalls the 2009 WHO consultation's positions on upholding ethics guidelines, the blurred line between practice and research, and adapting ethics oversight. It also explains how emergencies and disasters are understood, including natural and human-induced hazards, and ends with references.

sections.extract: Epidemics, emergencies and disasters raise many ethical issues for the people involved, who include responders, public health specialists and policy‑makers. This training manual provides material on ethical issues in research, surveillance and patient care in these difficult contexts, as well as related issues to reduce risks before, during and after events. summary.text: Sets out a 60-minute session on distinguishing public health surveillance from research, with team work on scenarios. The background defines public health and describes surveillance as a core activity that tracks disease patterns and guides control measures. It discusses why the line between research and surveillance is hard to draw, including tensions between informed consent and the goals of surveillance. The section closes with references and further reading.

The background explains that research is usually subject to independent ethics review while public health practice often is not. It outlines categories of research, such as clinical, health services and population-based studies, with examples, followed by references.

summary.text: Describes a 90-minute session on the ethical principles and requirements in current normative instruments for research and surveillance in emergencies. Participants read papers on what makes clinical research ethical, including in developing countries, before a presentation on major research ethics guidelines. The background traces the history of research ethics and the protections it offers participants, while noting debate about whether differences between research and public health practice should decide ethics review. References at the end include material on a disputed drug trial in Nigeria.

sections.title: Learning objective 1.4: Identify the shortcomings of current normative instruments for use in emergency situations, and evaluate alternatives.

summary.text: A training module, part of a course on ethics in emergencies and epidemics, on the shortcomings of existing research ethics guidelines and regulations when applied to emergencies. It gives a 120-minute session plan in which trainees test a guideline against a case study involving issues such as child vulnerability, consent across language barriers, confidentiality and conflicts of interest, then draft their own ethical framework. The background notes that most guidelines were written for clinical research in stable, well-resourced settings, while urgency in emergencies should not excuse ignoring core principles, citing the WHO panel on unregistered Ebola interventions. It then discusses altered perceptions of ethical issues, the patient–provider relationship, study integrity and ethics review, ending with references.

sections.title: Learning objective 2.1: Describe “standard” procedures that should govern an ethics review of research activities, including public health research.

summary.text: A training module describing the standard procedures that should govern ethics review of research, including public health research. Its 90-minute session plan uses a debate and a case that falls between research and surveillance to ask whether review standards could ever be altered and whether committee review is worth its cost. The background explains why prospective independent review is now broadly accepted, how multidisciplinary committees with lay members work and that review is not meant to obstruct research. It lists eleven areas a review should cover, from social value and informed consent to community participation, risk minimization and international collaboration, and ends with references and further reading.

sections.title: Learning objective 2.2: Identify circumstances in which public health surveillance activities should possibly undergo formal ethics review.

summary.text: A training module on when public health surveillance should undergo formal ethics review. Its 75-minute session plan uses a hospital testing case and group debate on which kinds of surveillance need review and which do not. The background explores the elusive line between surveillance and research, noting that research usually involves an intervention with quantifiable risk while much surveillance relies on data people may not know are collected. It discusses the ethical basis for oversight, including mutual responsibility, public trust and past misuse of HIV data, and ends by noting calls for risk-based rather than definition-based approaches, followed by references.

sections.title: Learning objective 2.3: Describe possible variations to standard procedures of ethics review that are applicable to research in emergencies.

summary.text: A training module on possible variations to standard ethics review procedures for research carried out during emergencies. Its 75-minute session plan combines group reflection, slides and two case studies asking whether projects are research or surveillance and whether expedited review or lighter consent procedures are acceptable. The background argues that research in emergencies is needed but must not exploit resource-poor settings, and sets out the debate over whether disaster survivors are inherently vulnerable. Proposed variations include expedited review, proportionality of risks and benefits, special scrutiny, generic anticipatory protocols and proactive review, with references at the end.

sections.title: Learning objective 3.1: Identify possible harm and benefit to individuals and communities resulting from public health practice and surveillance.

summary.text: A training module on the harms and benefits that public health practice and surveillance can bring to individuals and communities. Its 105-minute session plan includes writing exercises on when quarantine is justified, use of the Nuffield intervention ladder after an earthquake, a reading on the 1976 swine flu vaccine and a case about a surveillance survey that could fuel stigma. The background explains that, unlike in clinical care, benefits may go to the community while harms fall on individuals, illustrated by quarantine and mandatory vaccination. It stresses ethical practice as a way to build trust, as shown during the 2014 Ebola outbreak, and closes with references.

sections.title: Learning objective 3.2: Assess the factors to be considered in determining when public health surveillance requires explicit informed consent from individuals or communities.

summary.text: A training module on the factors that determine when public health surveillance requires explicit informed consent from individuals or communities. Its 60-minute session plan uses a case of a blood survey for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, with facilitator notes on whether it is research or surveillance, risks of identification and stigma, what information to disclose and whether patients may refuse. The background defines informed consent, notes its place in the Nuremberg Code, the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS guidelines, and sets out the arguments for it. It then considers when consent may be waived or modified, ending with references.

sections.title: Learning objective 3.3: Evaluate the measures required to protect privacy and confidentiality in an emergency.

summary.text: A training module on protecting privacy and confidentiality during emergencies. Its 90-minute session plan centres on a case in which a village leader asks a survey team for collected data, with suggested protective steps such as engaging leaders beforehand, avoiding identifiable data and transporting questionnaires in locked boxes. The background defines privacy and confidentiality and explains why emergencies threaten them, through less controlled settings, wider data sharing, improvised recording and limited resources for secure storage. It justifies the duty of confidentiality through beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy and trustworthiness, and ends with references.

sections.title: Learning objective 3.4: Describe specific measures required to protect and collect data and biological materials during public health surveillance.

summary.text: A training module on measures needed to protect data and biological materials collected during public health surveillance. Its 60-minute session plan uses a household blood-sampling case, with facilitator notes on what participants should be told, the risk of identifying positive individuals in small communities, safeguards such as broad geographical coding and restricted access, and whether results should be returned. The background describes ethical issues raised by specimens, including perceived intrusiveness, stigma that can extend to whole communities, and exploitation when products derived from samples are unaffordable locally, citing Indonesia's 2007 decision to stop sharing avian flu samples. References on stored biological materials close the section.

sections.title: Learning objective 3.5: Describe circumstances in which the common good might overrule individual autonomy during public health surveillance.

summary.text: A training module on circumstances in which the common good may override individual autonomy in public health surveillance. It sets out a 60-minute team-based case discussion and explains that measures such as surveillance, notification, mandatory testing or treatment and quarantine each infringe rights such as privacy, consent and freedom of movement. The background explains why autonomy matters ethically and discusses when such infringements can be justified, ending with references including Mill's On liberty.

sections.title: Learning objective 4.1: Identify potential harm and benefit to individuals and communities resulting from conducting research in emergencies.

summary.text: A training module on the potential harms and benefits to individuals and communities of conducting research during emergencies. Its 60-minute session plan has groups list harms and benefits, optionally view videos on the 1918 influenza pandemic, and discuss conflicting ethical principles and quotations on population health versus individual rights. The background notes that emergency research has sometimes caused disability and death, and raises questions about compromising scientific standards, who bears the risks of unapproved treatments and who gets first access to scarce new treatments. It stresses fair distribution of research benefits and burdens and barriers to valid consent in traditional or low-resource settings, ending with references including reports on drug trials in Nigeria.

sections.title: Learning objective 4.2: Discuss moral theories, and identify frameworks applicable to research in emergencies.

summary.text: Provides a 60-minute seminar plan for learning objective 4.2 on moral theories, in which the facilitator presents major ethical frameworks and leads discussion of their fit for research in emergencies. The background explains how utilitarianism, egalitarianism, libertarianism and rights-based theories each stress different values, and argues for a pluralistic approach. It then outlines a set of principles to weigh, each to be discussed in terms of justification, legitimacy and practicality, and closes with references including the Siracusa principles.

summary.text: Presents a 90-minute session for learning objective 4.4 on improving informed consent in emergency research, especially in traditional communities and low-resource settings. Participants read the Trovan case study and related news items, then split into groups to examine questions such as the ethical challenges of such settings and how the sponsor could have avoided wrongdoing. Facilitator notes cover language and cultural barriers, community permission, and the heightened vulnerability and risk of exploitation of participants during emergencies. The section includes background material and closes with references, including studies on consent comprehension in Ghana and clinical trial ethics in Nigeria.

summary.text: Outlines a 75-minute session for learning objective 5.1 on when data from surveillance or routine clinical care may be published as scientific knowledge, built around a role play in which the facilitator seeks post-hoc ethics clearance for a paper by Balasegaram et al. Groups decide whether to grant clearance, weighing the lack of patient information and prior ethics review against social benefit. Background text stresses the strong obligation to share emergency findings quickly, and the section ends with references.

sections.title: Learning objective 5.2: Explain what is meant by “publication bias” and how it might affect the response to emergencies.

summary.text: Gives a 90-minute session plan for learning objective 5.2 on publication bias and its effect on emergency response, combining readings by Godlee and Loder and by Cohen, a news video about the antiviral Tamiflu, and a case study. Small groups discuss whether the case shows publication bias, how it could be prevented or mitigated, and how it could affect emergency response. Background material explains that emergency preparedness relies on research evidence and describes proposed methods for addressing publication bias. References at the end include WHO documents on H5N1 influenza and the Model List of Essential Medicines.

sections.title: Learning objective 5.3: Explain the ethical obligations of researchers, public health practitioners and publishers regarding ownership of scientific data.

summary.text: Presents a 120-minute session for learning objective 5.3 on the ethical obligations of researchers, public health practitioners and publishers regarding ownership of scientific data. After readings and a video about Tamiflu, two groups debate stricter data control versus open data sharing during an emergency, to inform thinking about data-sharing policy. Participants then examine a case study on access to data on oseltamivir effectiveness, weighing data ownership against public benefit. The section closes with references and further reading on drug safety and effectiveness.

summary.text: Introduces core competence 6, on ethical criteria for triage, resource allocation and standards of care in emergency response, illustrated by a photo from the 2010 Haiti earthquake. It lists four learning objectives covering triage and rationing frameworks, altered standards of care, benefit-sharing with communities under surveillance, and equitable access to unproven treatments.

sections.title: Learning objective 6.1: Discuss ethical frameworks and criteria for triage and rationing in emergencies.

summary.text: Sets out a 90-minute session for learning objective 6.1 on ethical frameworks and criteria for triage and rationing in emergencies. Small groups consider questions such as which resources may need allocating, who should make triage decisions, which criteria should never be used, and whether to maximize lives or life-years saved. Further large-group discussion and a reading follow, with background on triage criteria and conflicts between the common good and individual patients. The section ends with references, including WHO discussion papers on ethics in pandemic influenza planning.

sections.title: Learning objective 6.2: Understand how criteria for standards of care and treatment can be altered during emergencies.

summary.text: Provides a 90-minute session for learning objective 6.2 on how standards of care and treatment may be altered during emergencies, distinguishing this from triage. The first case study uses an article and video about Dr Anna Pou's actions in a hospital after a hurricane to explore moral versus legal responsibility. A second exercise uses scenarios from Levin et al. for individual reflection and group discussion, and the section closes with references.

sections.title: Learning objective 6.3: Identify issues of benefit‑sharing with communities under public health surveillance.

summary.text: Outlines a 105-minute session for learning objective 6.3 on benefit-sharing with communities under public health surveillance, starting with the UNESCO Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights and the line between benefits and undue inducement. Participants read Simm (2007) and discuss in groups how benefit-sharing applies to surveillance, followed by a case presentation and discussion. Background covers the history of the benefit-sharing concept. References include the Nagoya Protocol, WHO's Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework and the Declaration of Helsinki.

sections.title: Learning objective 6.4: Identify issues of equity of access to unproven treatments during research in the course of emergency response.

summary.text: Sets out a 60-minute session with reading and a debate for learning objective 6.4 on equitable access to unproven treatments during emergency research. The case study concerns post-exposure prophylaxis during an Ebola outbreak in central Africa and the tension between generating robust trial data and compassionate use to save lives now. Facilitator notes refer to the 2014 west African Ebola epidemic and a WHO panel convened that August on the ethics of investigational interventions. The section ends with references on trial designs and the ethics of experimental Ebola treatments.

sections.title: Learning objective 7.1: Distinguish three ethics frameworks: medical care ethics, public health ethics and research ethics, and explore the ways in which the values and principles that guide these frameworks diverge or overlap.

summary.text: Presents a training session plan for learning objective 7.1, which asks trainees to compare the aims, values and principles of medical care ethics, public health ethics and research ethics. The 100-minute session moves from an introduction through small-group work with a comparison template, a video on disaster ethics, a case study, a role-play and a closing summary. Facilitator notes supply discussion questions on whether clinical values can be carried into public health interventions and research in emergencies. The section ends with a list of readings and references on clinical, public health and disaster ethics.

sections.title: Learning objective 7.2: Explain what is meant by “therapeutic misconception” and how it could affect the duties of health care workers in emergencies.

summary.text: Sets out a 75-minute training session on the concept of therapeutic misconception and how it bears on the duties of health care workers who take part in research during emergencies. Facilitators introduce the idea, review three strategies for helping people tell clinical research apart from medical care, and ask participants whether these are workable given language barriers, trauma and scarce resources. A case study and role-play follow, with questions on how the misconception arises and how a physician might reduce it. The section closes with references, including qualitative studies of research participation and work on empirical bioethics.

sections.title: Learning objective 7.3: Explain the potential conflicts of interest of health care workers participating in emergency research activities.

summary.text: Provides a 90-minute, highly interactive session plan on conflicts of interest faced by health care workers who join research activities during emergencies. The facilitator presents definitions, then problem-solving tools for identifying, evaluating and managing such conflicts, and a model for handling them ethically. A multi-part case study is revealed in stages, with a discussion guide steering the group through three phases of analysis. The section ends with references on research integrity and responsible conduct of research.

sections.title: Glossary

summary.text: A glossary that defines common concepts, principles and values used in health ethics, noting that the definitions are aids to understanding rather than definitive. Entries include terms such as accountability for reasonableness, autonomy and beneficence, each with supporting citations. It opens with a photo caption about WHO support to a hospital medical records office in Sri Lanka and ends with a numbered reference list.

sections.title: Annex II. Case studies

summary.text: Annex II collects the case studies used throughout the course on ethics in epidemics, emergencies and disasters, grouped by core competence and cross-referenced to the sessions that use them. The first case asks groups how to allocate scarce intravenous fluid sets during an outbreak of viral haemorrhagic fever with limited diagnostic capacity. Later cases cover topics drawn from the course objectives, each followed by discussion questions on how problems might have been handled differently. The annex ends with contact details for WHO's Global Health Ethics Unit.

narratives.en: Figure 1, research to improve health systems (Remme et al., 2010): a three-band diagram. Research domains are shown as nested brackets of increasing size: operational, implementation and health system. Their corresponding users are health care providers, programme managers, and health system managers/policy makers, and a widening wedge shows research utility ranging from local to broad.
narratives.ar: الشكل 1، البحوث الرامية إلى تحسين النظم الصحية (Remme وآخرون، 2010): مخطط من ثلاثة نطاقات. تُعرض مجالات البحث على شكل أقواس متداخلة متزايدة الحجم: البحوث التشغيلية، وبحوث التنفيذ، وبحوث النظم الصحية. ومستخدموها المقابلون هم مقدمو الرعاية الصحية، ومديرو البرامج، ومديرو النظم الصحية/واضعو السياسات، ويبيّن إسفين متّسع أن فائدة البحث تتدرج من محلية إلى واسعة.
narratives.zh: 图1：改善卫生系统的研究（Remme等，2010）：三栏图。研究领域以逐渐增大的嵌套括号表示：业务研究、实施研究和卫生系统研究。对应的使用者为卫生保健提供者、规划管理人员以及卫生系统管理人员/政策制定者；一个逐渐变宽的楔形表示研究效用从局部到广泛。
narratives.es: Figura 1, investigación para mejorar los sistemas de salud (Remme et al., 2010): diagrama de tres franjas. Los ámbitos de investigación se muestran como corchetes anidados de tamaño creciente: operativa, de implementación y de sistemas de salud. Sus usuarios correspondientes son los prestadores de atención de salud, los gestores de programas y los gestores de sistemas de salud/responsables de políticas, y una cuña que se ensancha muestra la utilidad de la investigación, de local a amplia.
narratives.fr: Figure 1, recherche pour l'amélioration des systèmes de santé (Remme et al., 2010) : diagramme en trois bandes. Les domaines de recherche sont représentés par des crochets emboîtés de taille croissante : opérationnelle, de mise en œuvre et sur les systèmes de santé. Leurs utilisateurs correspondants sont les prestataires de soins, les gestionnaires de programmes et les gestionnaires des systèmes de santé/décideurs, et un coin qui s'élargit montre l'utilité de la recherche, de locale à large.
narratives.ru: Рисунок 1 — исследования для совершенствования систем здравоохранения (Remme et al., 2010): диаграмма из трёх полос. Области исследований показаны вложенными скобками возрастающего размера: операционные исследования, исследования внедрения и исследования систем здравоохранения. Соответствующие пользователи — поставщики медицинской помощи, руководители программ и руководители систем здравоохранения/лица, формирующие политику; расширяющийся клин показывает полезность исследований — от местной до широкой.

tables.caption: Table 1. Core ethical principles and issues covered by the main guidelines and examples of their application in emergencies

columns.titles: Examples of guidelines that address the ethical principle or issue

rows: Respect for people’s autonomy

The duty to respect people’s ability to make decisions on issues related to their health and their body, if they are competent to make such decisions; and the duty to protect individuals with impaired or diminished autonomy
Obtaining informed consent from people affected by an emergency before their identifiable personal information or biological samples are collected and processed for research purposes
CIOMS, General principles; Tri-Council Policy Statement, article 1.1; Belmont Report, Basic ethical principles
Informed consent

A process whereby potential research participants decide whether they want to participate in the proposed study after receiving information about it. The requirements for consent considered to be valid vary by guideline and regulation. In general, they agree that decisions must be made free from coercion, by a competent person who can understand the information given and appreciate the associated risks. The information given to the participant should be in a language and format suitable to the participant’s ability to comprehend it.
CIOMS, General principles, guidelines 4–6; Declaration of Helsinki, privacy and confidentiality, articles 25–32; Tri-Council Policy Statement, Chapter 3, The consent process
Beneficence
The moral duty to pursue actions that promote the well-being of others and the ethical obligation to maximize benefit and to minimize harm
To benefit from and have access to a vaccine in a pandemic
CIOMS, General principles; Belmont Report, Basic ethical principles
Non-maleficence
The moral duty not to cause harm to others through interventions
Vaccine trials should involve the fewest human subjects and the fewest tests on those subjects that will ensure scientifically valid data.
CIOMS, General principles; Declaration of Helsinki, Risks, burdens and benefits (articles 16–18)
Justice

Primarily distributive justice, which requires equitable distribution of benefits and burdens, i.e. distribution such that no segment of the population is unduly burdened by the harms of research or denied the benefits of the knowledge generated from it
Collecting samples from citizens of a developing country affected by a pandemic in order to develop a vaccine rapidly and ensure that the vaccine is made fairly available locally

CIOMS, General principles, guidelines 10 and 12; Declaration of Helsinki, Risks, burdens and benefits, articles 16–18; Tri-Council Policy Statement, article 1.1 and Chapter 4, Fairness and equity in research participation
Vulnerability

A status in which some people may struggle to protect their interests or be at greater risk of being exploited. This situation is usually linked to specific physical, financial, educational or social circumstances. Groups considered as vulnerable vary by guideline, but children, mentally and/or physically disabled individuals, prisoners, refugees, terminally ill patients and women are often cited as the prime vulnerable groups.
Targeting women and children for surveillance during emergencies without epidemiological or methodological justification

CIOMS, General principles, guidelines 13–16; Declaration of Helsinki, Vulnerable groups and individuals, articles 19 and 20; Common rule, subparts B, C and D; Tri-Council Policy Statement, Chapter 9, Research involving the First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples of Canada
Privacy

The right or expectation not to be interfered with or to be free from surveillance or, more generally, a moral right to be left alone. In practical terms, privacy is for instance concerned with the setting in which a person’s health-related information is acquired.
Taking precautions to interview victims of an emergency in private places (i.e. where those not related to the study cannot see or hear them)
Tri-Council Policy Statement, Chapter 5, Privacy and confidentiality; Declaration of Helsinki, Privacy and confidentiality, article 24
Confidentiality

The principle that ensures that identifiable information is kept out of reach of others. All identifiable information about individuals, whether recorded (written, computerized, visual, audio) or simply held in the memory of health professionals, is subject to the duty of confidentiality.
Ensuring that identifiable data from surveillance activities are secured and not accessible by irrelevant persons (e.g. locked in filing cabinets or in encrypted files)
CIOMS, Guideline 18, Safeguarding confidentiality; Tri-Council Policy Statement, Chapter 5, Privacy and confidentiality
tables.notes: 1 These definitions are not universal. The author tried to capture the main, or the common, features of each concept. Different guidelines may have different definitions for each of these principles. Moreover, the literature on research ethics has different approaches and definitions. One comprehensive, simple-to-use resource that provides more information on these concepts is the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Zalta, 2014). narratives.en: Eight core research-ethics principles and issues (autonomy, informed consent, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, vulnerability, privacy, confidentiality), each with a definition, an example of its application in emergencies and examples of guidelines that address it (CIOMS, Declaration of Helsinki, Belmont Report, Tri-Council Policy Statement, Common Rule).
narratives.ar: ثمانية مبادئ وقضايا أساسية في أخلاقيات البحث (الاستقلالية، والموافقة المستنيرة، والإحسان، وعدم الإضرار، والعدالة، والاستضعاف، والخصوصية، والسرية)، مع تعريف كل منها ومثال على تطبيقه في حالات الطوارئ وأمثلة على المبادئ التوجيهية التي تتناوله (مجلس المنظمات الدولية للعلوم الطبية، وإعلان هلسنكي، وتقرير بلمونت، وبيان السياسات للمجالس الثلاثة، والقاعدة المشتركة).
narratives.zh: 八项核心研究伦理原则和问题（自主、知情同意、有益、不伤害、公正、脆弱性、隐私、保密），每项均给出定义、在突发事件中的应用示例以及涉及该原则的指南示例（国际医学科学组织理事会、《赫尔辛基宣言》、《贝尔蒙报告》、三理事会政策声明、通用规则）。
narratives.es: Ocho principios y cuestiones fundamentales de ética de la investigación (autonomía, consentimiento informado, beneficencia, no maleficencia, justicia, vulnerabilidad, privacidad, confidencialidad), cada uno con su definición, un ejemplo de aplicación en emergencias y ejemplos de directrices que lo abordan (CIOMS, Declaración de Helsinki, Informe Belmont, Declaración de Política de los Tres Consejos, Common Rule).
narratives.fr: Huit principes et questions fondamentaux de l’éthique de la recherche (autonomie, consentement éclairé, bienfaisance, non-malfaisance, justice, vulnérabilité, vie privée, confidentialité), chacun avec sa définition, un exemple d’application dans les situations d’urgence et des exemples de lignes directrices qui le traitent (CIOMS, Déclaration d’Helsinki, Rapport Belmont, Énoncé de politique des trois Conseils, Common Rule).
narratives.ru: Восемь основных принципов и вопросов этики исследований (автономия, информированное согласие, благодеяние, непричинение вреда, справедливость, уязвимость, неприкосновенность частной жизни, конфиденциальность) с определением каждого, примером применения в чрезвычайных ситуациях и примерами руководств, в которых они рассматриваются (CIOMS, Хельсинкская декларация, Белмонтский доклад, Совместное заявление о политике трех советов, Common Rule).
